review_text_raw:
"Cyber Manhunt" is a visual novel disguised as a detective game: it has a few timed puzzles and optional information, but in general the game is linear.
The story is far from perfect: it is too dark and not depressing enough at the same time to be realistic. The ending chapter is just meh. The gameplay has a few shortcomings: the in-game desktop is not responsive enough, the data gathering process is tedious, and the puzzles can be bothersome given the running timer. The stylization is fine, I guess, until it comes to anything computer-related (Of course, it is of little importance, but now I know that viruses are always written in C and bash while any database with private data utilizes systemd. Wait. What?) The English translation is sub-par and has lots of typos.
It is a bit sad, because I see the potential in this game, but I cannot recommend it.

So, I got this game because it reminded me a lot of Orwell. I've grown to like playing detective games where you learn more about others through their media and all that. And yeah, I know this is a hacking game and different, but it's clear this game was inspired by Orwell, at least to me it was. Now, first going into this, the game was kind of fun. Simple, but fun. It does seem to get harder as you go along and it's interesting to learn more about the chapter your in. 

However, the game has two major problems for me. First off, the interface is a bit annoying. Like, to erase something, you need to actually hit your own delete button. I know this may be nitpicking, but you don't have to do this when copying and pasting, and you are going to be doing a lot of these two. It's also tedious going through the apps. When closing them, for example, you have to recopy  the password in should you need to go back to the same users file. 

Another thing that makes this game a bit annoying for me is the tutorial. This game, unless your good with tech and/or hacking, doesn't do a good job at explaining certain aspects of the game. A good example of this is when you need to hack into someone's phone in chapter two. It's also vaguely explains certain things later in the game and this is done by your jerk of the boss. I don't get this since the beginning had a pretty nice tutorial. 

I don't want to say it's a bad game. It's not actually. But honestly, the interface and lacking tutorial for later and important parts of the game make this not fun for me. If you're someone who doesn't care much for these things or good with tech/hacking,  I'll think you'll enjoy it. The game is lacking a bit though in terms of really getting into these peoples' life and getting to know them. I wish it had done more of that because the chapters are interesting. Still, I'll change my review should these two things be changed (or at least the interface.) It's not a bad game and is decent, but for me at the moment I don't want to keep playing it.

review_text_raw:
The execution needs work. 

I enjoy Orwell and other games in this vein. My main issue here is that it's tedious. It doesn't show you which information it wants you to click on until you mouse over it. But sometimes clearly important information isn't clickable. Other times information will be essential to click, but it's unclear exactly why. The result is that you have to mouse over everything, relevant or not. If you missed something, you have to search everywhere again to find it. 

The result was me being in a place where I knew all the answers and had solved everything, but wasn't allowed to end the level because I had missed clicking on some piece of information somewhere. I looked at important pieces of information multiple times, and eventually found that the piece I had missed was something that was only slightly relevant to the situation at hand. 

In other words- it didn't make me feel like I was solving puzzles. It made me feel like I was trying every single option whether it made sense or not, because that was the only way to progress. When I got stuck, it wasn't because I couldn't figure something out or because I didn't understand, it was because there was some random thing that I hadn't realized it wanted me to do.

Really disappointed about this game. I was hoping for some good sleuthing, but as I've read in other reviews the game soon becomes hovering your mouse over text to find predefined clues, reading content optional. All other game mechanics reach like 10% of their potential:
- "googling" for clues: you can really only search for people's names, everything else returns "not found"
- hacking passwords: copy/paste info from another window and click the button
- phishing: you have to trial and error until you find the random sequence they imagined
Aside from that, getting into emails and other accounts, all gets repetitive really fast. 
About translations: I read about other reviewers complaining about the English. When I purchased the game they had just released improved translations, but there is still much work to do...
Last point: what I would have liked to see, is a much more open gameplay, where one has to read everything to find clues, take their own notes, and has chances to make mistakes so that there is at least an illusion that the path to success isn't linear.

review_text_raw:
I wanted to like this game as it's clear that quite a bit of effort was put into making it, and (at least at the date of this review) the developer is still trying to improve on it.  The graphics are nice and I like this genre of game.  Game play length is decent, you can complete it within 9-10 hours at a leisurely pace.

Having said that, I can't bring myself to recommend it.  The worst part of the game is the writing. Aside from some translation and grammatical errors which I can ignore, the nicest way I can put it is that the writing style is simply not for me. The characters are so incredibly tropey, dramatic and honestly cringey in the way they speak. The twists and turns are juvenile and the themes are simplistic and shallow. The game doesn't say anything you don't already know (i.e. wouldn't it be bad if hackers are able to use your private data on social media for nefarious means? Really makes you think!).

Aside from the writing, the game play is okay though fairly repetitive.  The game does try to keep you engaged with new mini games that pop up, though at least one puzzle right at the end of the game is completely frustrating in a way that makes no sense and when you're under time pressure as well. By that point, I just wanted the game to be finished.

I'm sure there's an audience for this game (maybe younger people?) but it's not for me unfortunately.

The game really can't decide if it wants to be puzzly or hold your hand constantly, even artificially blocking your progression until it deems you "ready".

The UX is outright abyssmal, with every action having some sort of artificial delay, like waiting for some voice line to finish, or have an arbitrary fake progress bar go up. This will happen dozens and dozens of times. It can not be turned off. It can not be skipped.

It adds up to a LOT of time wasted, even if you aren't forced to repeat them because of the random minute "quizzes" the game occasionally throws at you, marking the only time where the game won't let you look up anything. You remember exactly WHERE the info would be, but no - you have to game over, retry, look it up, go through 1 or 2 minutes of unskippable very mediocre voiced lines again, and only THEN are you allowed to progress... to the next question. Rinse and repeat, unless you literally memorized every single little remark and detail from dozens of random conversations and social media posts.

The game ist just so incredibly tedious to play. It actively doesn't want you to have any fun. The story could be decent enough I guess, but it's certainly not enough of a payoff for the awful, awful gameplay.

There is a lot to like, but overall I wouldn't _recommend_ this game.

First off, in my perspective, timers ruin most everything that could be fun. Life is busy, interruptions pop up. In this game, one cannot pause and there's not a lot of time allowed for dilly dallying. Always seems a silly way of trying to make something challenging, having to do it faster. The timed parts are simple enough, and seem to be re-doable, but they're not enjoyable that way.  Nearer the end in particular are some puzzles that would be much more enjoyable without a timer or at least with a pause button.

What possibly contributed to souring my experience 
I wound up having to play a bunch of the game over twice, because first I couldn't make any of the boxes on the screen move, during a timed event. After click click clicking all around, I restarted. The game seemed like it was picking up just before the timed part, but nothing I did could trigger the timed part. nothing would happen. So, I restarted from a manual save point. Then, before I caught back up to where I had been, I inadvertently closed a window that then wouldn't open again, and the game proceeded as though I had made a different choice, so I went back to my manual save point again because I didn't want that. Through that experience, I became more aware how tedious the copying and pasting can be.

It is very close to being a game I would recommend and I wouldn't tell anybody not to get it. The price isn't at all bad. I just got too irritated at not being able to pause those timed parts to complete it.

2/5

Cyber Manhunt falls disappointingly short of what I was expecting. While it's evident that the developers poured time and effort into this game, the end result is a mediocre experience. Nothing is horribly bad, but nothing is great either.

One of the major letdowns is the story line, which is... cliched. I could figure out where it was going almost beat-for-beat. The characters feel two-dimensional, and most of the time I could skip past their dialogue and just find the highlighted bits I was meant to find without losing anything meaningful from the parts I skipped. 
Sleuthing, he game's core mechanic, turns out to be a painfully limited and repetitive experience. The investigative elements promised are reduced to basic point-and-click tasks, and copy-and-pasting things into boxes. The puzzles lack complexity and fail to challenge the player's intellect, resulting a cycle that gets old after chapter 2.
The dialogue delivery is often wooden, making it difficult to immerse oneself in the story.

I can tell the devs really tried, which redeems this to a point, but the overall experience falls flat. With a more engaging story line and more diverse detective mechanics, Cyber Manhunt could have been a standout title.

It's "meh". The gameplay is composed of two types of puzzles: 
1. The repetitive: this is the bulk of it. Repeat the exact same steps to "hack" each account, etc. 
2. The one-time-puzzles: some of these are trivial, and some (especially towards the end) are guesswork.
Towards the end some puzzles are even pure guesswork if you want to make it to the "good" ending. 

All in all, the story is nice - not great, but nice. The game is very repetitive. Wouldn't recommend. You played 2 episodes? you're good. This is most of the game really.
